claims.claim: Le Guin states as a principle of narrative description that listing is not describing and that only the relevant belongs.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft: A Twenty-First-Century Guide to Sailing the Sea of Story (Mariner Books / Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2015)
claims.quote: Listing is not describing. Only the relevant belongs.

claims.claim: Le Guin says what a writer leaves out is infinitely more than what is left in.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft: A Twenty-First-Century Guide to Sailing the Sea of Story (Mariner Books / Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2015)
claims.quote: what you leave out is infinitely more than what you leave in

claims.claim: Le Guin says there has to be white space around the word and silence around the voice.

verdicts.trueWording: first published by Eighth Mountain in 1998; revised Mariner 2015
verdicts.note: Raw HTML of ursulakleguin.com/steering-the-craft fetched (HTTP 200, browser UA). Publication note reads verbatim: 'Steering the Craft was first published by Eighth Mountain in 1998; the revised edition was published by Mariner in 2015.' Both limbs (Eighth Mountain/1998, Mariner/2015) supported; page adds it is currently published by Harper Perennial.

verdicts.trueWording: Pendragon Press 'in 1973 published it in a limited run of 776 copies'
verdicts.note: Raw HTML of ursulakleguin.com/from-elfland-to-poughkeepsie fetched (HTTP 200). Page: 'the text of a speech Ursula gave at the Second Annual Science Fiction Writers' Workshop in 1972 ... It was the first book published by Pendragon Press (Portland), who in 1973 published it in a limited run of 776 copies.' All three limbs (1972 workshop, Pendragon 1973, 776 copies) supported; page also notes 1975 (1006) and 1978 (2000) reprints.

verdicts.trueWording: 'Listing is not describing. Only the relevant belongs.'
verdicts.note: Raw djvu text of the 2015 Mariner edition fetched from archive.org (HTTP 200, 221,397 bytes). Quote appears word for word in chapter 10 'Crowding and Leaping' (chapter numbering confirmed: heading '10. crowding and leaping'), in the paragraph on leaping and description.

verdicts.trueWording: 'what you leave out is infinitely more than what you leave in'
verdicts.note: Same raw djvu text. Full sentence: 'And what you leave out is infinitely more than what you leave in.' Chapter 10, immediately after 'What you leap over is what you leave out.'

verdicts.trueWording: 'There's got to be white space around the word, silence around the voice.'
verdicts.note: Same raw djvu text. The quoted fragment appears verbatim inside that sentence; the claim's 'there has to be' renders the book's 'There's got to be' — same proposition, chapter 10.

verdicts.trueWording: 'never to use ten vague words where two exact words will do'
verdicts.note: Same raw djvu text. Verbatim, and it is indeed a gloss of crowding: 'Crowding is what Keats meant ... It's what we mean when we exhort ourselves to avoid flabby language and cliches, never to use ten vague words where two exact words will do, always to seek the vivid phrase, the exact word.' Chapter 10.

verdicts.trueWording: 'Overcrowded descriptions clog the story and suffocate themselves.'
verdicts.note: Same raw djvu text. Verbatim sentence, chapter 10, following the Funes the Memorious reference and preceding the Flaubert/Salammbo aside.

verdicts.trueWording: 'Everything the reader needs to know is included, but nothing more.'
verdicts.note: Same raw djvu text. Verbatim, and the O'Brian attribution limb is supported by the preceding sentence: 'For a magnificent example of action writing, look at any of the sea battles in Patrick O'Brian's Aubrey-Maturin novels.' Chapter 10.

verdicts.trueWording: 'The sensory details are intense, brief, precise.'
verdicts.note: Same raw djvu text. Verbatim, three sentences after the Patrick O'Brian sea-battle sentence, so the praise-of-O'Brian limb is supported by the same passage. Chapter 10.

verdicts.trueWording: 'There is no optimum sentence length. The optimum is variety.'
verdicts.note: Same raw djvu text. Both sentences verbatim in chapter 3 (heading '3. sentence length and complex syntax'), followed by 'The length of a sentence in good prose is established by contrast and interplay with the sentences around it.'

verdicts.trueWording: 'the only good sentence is a short sentence. ... I don't.'
verdicts.note: Same raw djvu text. Every limb supported: 'Teachers trying to get kids to write understandably, textbooks of style with their notion of "transparent" style, journalists with their weird rules and superstitions, and bang-pow thriller writers - they've all helped filled a lot of heads with the notion that the only good sentence is a short sentence. A convicted criminal might agree. I don't.' Chapter 3.

verdicts.trueWording: 'It's a myth that short-sentence prose is "more like the way we speak."'
verdicts.note: Same raw djvu text. Quoted fragment verbatim; the completing phrase 'more like the way we speak' appears on the page in the book's own quotation marks. Chapter 3, after the 'See Spot. See Jane.' example.

verdicts.trueWording: 'In a narrative, the chief duty of a sentence is to lead to the next sentence.'
verdicts.note: Same raw djvu text. Verbatim, and it is the opening sentence of chapter 3 ('3. sentence length and complex syntax'), so the 'in a narrative' limb is supported.

verdicts.trueWording: 'A sentence isn't working as a narrative sentence if ... its similes or metaphors so dazzling, that it stops the reader'
verdicts.note: Same raw djvu text. Every limb of the claim is supported verbatim on the page: 'A sentence isn't working as a narrative sentence if its order is so unexpected, or its adjectives and adverbs so striking, or its similes* or metaphors* so dazzling, that it stops the reader, even to say "Ooh!"'. CAVEAT ON THE ATTACHED QUOTE: the claim's quote field, 'the proper beauty and power of prose', is also verbatim on the page but belongs to a different, later sentence ('though every sentence should move with grace, the proper beauty and power of prose is in the work as a whole') and does not by itself evidence the claim. Graded VERIFIED_VERBATIM because both rubric conditions hold (quote word-for-word on page; every limb supported), but the citation should be re-pointed to the sentence given in trueWording. Located in the chapter-2 'Conjunctivitis' passage on killing your darlings, not chapter 3 as the page field states.

verdicts.trueWording: 'ADJECTIVES AND ADVERBS ARE RICH AND good and nourishing ... cause obesity in prose only when used lazily or overused.'
verdicts.note: Same raw djvu text. Both limbs supported. The sidebar's OCR is split across a page break: the opening runs 'ADJECTIVES AND ADVERBS ARE RICH AND good and nourishing. They ... add color, life, immediacy. They cause obesity in prose only when' (line 1695) while its tail 'used lazily or overused.' was OCR'd out of order to line 1661, just under the '5. adjectives and adverbs' chapter heading. Reassembled, the sidebar reads exactly as the claim states. Quote field matches word for word including the drop-cap capitalization.
